summary: Defines the Content-Language header to indicate the language of content and the Accept-Language header for stating a preference. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This is a label saying what language a page is in, and a way for you to ask for the language you want.

questions: how to indicate language of content
how do q values work in accept-language
subtitle: Two small mail-style headers: one labels the language of content, the other states which languages you prefer.

tldr.problem: People want information in a language they understand, and programs need a way to label what language some content is in and to say which languages a user prefers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3282 defines a Content-Language header that lists language tags for content, and an Accept-Language header that lists preferred language ranges, optionally with quality values. Both work wherever RFC 822-like headers are used, such as MIME body parts or Web documents.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1766 and moves the language tag definition out into RFC 3066. It is a Draft Standard and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 3282 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1766, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the language tag definition in RFC 3066.

sections.title: Why Label Languages
sections.content:
Many people would prefer information in a language they understand. Sometimes the same information exists in several languages, or tools such as dictionaries can help. Sometimes a program might convert text into another form, such as computer-synthesized speech or Braille.

All of that needs a label that says which language the content uses. The language tags themselves are defined elsewhere (the RFC calls that reference [TAGS], which is RFC 3066). RFC 3282 only defines the protocol elements that carry those tags in protocols with RFC 822-like headers.
sections.eli5: Before anyone can pick the right book, every book needs a sticker saying what language it is in. This document says how to write the sticker.

sections.title: The Content-Language Header
sections.content:
The Content-Language header says which language or languages something is in. It is meant for anything with RFC 822-like headers, such as MIME body parts or Web documents. The header may list several languages in a comma-separated list.

The RFC gives the grammar in two forms: the older RFC 822 EBNF, and the stricter RFC 2234 ABNF. The ABNF allows CFWS, which works like the whitespace convention in RFC 822, so parenthesized comments and continuation lines can appear in the list.

A looser obs-content-language grammar is also given. Following RFC 2822, implementations MUST accept it but MUST NOT generate it. Everything an implementation generates has to follow the strict syntax.
sections.eli5: The sticker can name more than one language, separated by commas. Be strict when you write the sticker, but be relaxed when you read one that someone else wrote a bit sloppily.

sections.title: Examples of Content-Language Values
sections.content:
The RFC shows the header next to a Content-type line. A voice recording from Liverpool downtown uses en-scouse. A document in Mingo, an American Indian language with no ISO 639 code, uses i-mingo. A Star Trek excerpt uses i-klingon.

A list shows content in more than one language. An English-French dictionary is labelled en, fr (This is a dictionary), with a comment in parentheses. An official European Commission document in several of its languages is labelled da, de, el, en, fr, it.
sections.eli5: A sticker can say one language, like English, or a few at once. It can even say Klingon.

sections.title: The Accept-Language Header
sections.content:
The Accept-Language header lets a user or a process name the languages it prefers. It lists language ranges, whose syntax and meaning come from the language tag document, separated by commas. Each range may carry a quality value written q= after a semicolon.

If no q values are given, the ranges are in priority order and the leftmost is the most preferred. The RFC calls this an extension to the HTTP/1.1 rules that matches current practice. If q values are given, the details of how to evaluate them are in HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616).

As with the other header, a liberal obsolete grammar exists. Implementations MUST accept it and MUST NOT generate it.
sections.eli5: Accept-Language is your list of favorite languages. If you do not give scores, the first one on the list is your favorite.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 1766 said security issues were believed to be irrelevant. Since then one concern has been raised: language ranges used in content negotiation could be used to infer the nationality of the sender, and so identify potential targets for surveillance.

The RFC treats this as a special case of the general fact that anything you send is visible to the receiving party. The size of the threat, and any countermeasures, are left to each application protocol. A short section on character sets adds nothing beyond what the language tag document says.
sections.eli5: If you tell a website your favorite languages, it learns a little about you. Be aware of that.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1766
sections.content:
RFC 3282 obsoletes RFC 1766. The definition of language tags was split out and is now RFC 3066.

The differences parameter to multipart/alternative is no longer part of the standard, because no implementations of the function were ever found. The RFC points readers who need it back to RFC 1766. The ABNF for Content-Language was updated to the RFC 2234 style.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook was split into two smaller books, and one rule nobody ever used was thrown out.

data.title: Content-Language examples
data.code:
Content-type: application/dictionary
Content-Language: en, fr (This is a dictionary)

Content-type: multipart/alternative
Content-Language: da, de, el, en, fr, it
